papers.title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1, encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1{triangleup} mutants lack {beta}-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

papers.title: Characterisation of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei hybrids for oenological applications
papers.abstract: The Saccharomyces genus present as a genetically diverse set of microorganisms capable of tolerating a range of environmental stressors, demonstrating high fermentation capacity and producing interesting flavour compounds. Such diversity can be exploited in a single organism by producing interspecies hybrids, overcoming the limitations of a single species. Here, as proof of principle, we exploited a library of F12 interspecies diploid hybrids between Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei (Sc/Sj), to identify new strains harbouring traits of oenological relevance, such as ethanol and glycerol production, superior tolerance to acetic acid, limited production of H2S, and optimal growth on fructose. Moreover, we calculated robustness across strains tested on solid media comparing the trade-off between performance on a single conditions and overall robustness. Progeny from a range of robustness values with favourable H2S production profiles were isolated for further analysis via micro and small-scale fermentations. Micro-scale fermentations in synthetic grape must containing individual wine-associated stressors were performed, and the robustness of the selected strains was confirmed. The wine characteristics of the hybrids were tested in small-scale fermentations in synthetic grape media. We found that both ethanol and glycerol production across our selected progeny matched or exceeding that from the commercial wine strain, and most hybrids produced less acetic acid and more fatty-acids, including higher quantities of associated esters. Overall, we were able to identify suitable Sc/Sj hybrids with interesting aroma profiles to develop further for wine fermentation.

papers.title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya and related parahenipaviruses
papers.abstract: Langya virus is a zoonotic parahenipavirus with pandemic potential that causes acute febrile illness in people. We identified endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) as an entry receptor for Langya, Wenzhou, and Mojiang parahenipaviruses. A 3.1 [A] cryo-electron microscopy structure reveals that Langya attachment glycoprotein engages EPCR through a site distinct from that of the ephrin binding site of Nipah G. This binding mode resembles those of protein C and a malarial adhesin, demonstrating convergent evolution. Interface substitutions abolish entry, whereas natural variation explains differential human EPCR use and predicts receptor compatibility across 26 animal species. These findings establish EPCR as a receptor for the Langya clade and provide a structural framework for understanding cross-species transmission and human infection potential.

papers.title: APR-246 and DNA polymerase theta inhibitor Novobiocinsynergize to eliminate TP53 mutant AML cells
papers.abstract: Patients with TP53-mutant myelodysplasic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are usually elderly and frail with highly resistant malignant clones and a median survival of less than one year. The molecule APR-246 targets mutant p53 but also perturbs redox homeostasis. APR-246 showed favorable safety in a phase 3 trial in TP53 mutant MDS/AML but did not meet efficacy endpoints in combination with azacitidine (AZA), highlighting the need for more effective combination strategies. Conversion of APR-246 to the active compound MQ releases formaldehyde which generates DNA-protein crosslinks. AML cells depend on DNA polymerase theta (Pol[O]) to repair such lesions and Pol[O] protects cells from ferroptosis. Using a panel of isogenic MOLM13 AML cell lines each carrying a common TP53 variant, we show that the Pol[O] inhibitor Novobiocin (NVB) synergizes with APR-246 to induce AML cell death. We demonstrate strong synergy with this combination in all TP53 mutant cell lines and to a lesser extent in the TP53 wildtype and null cells, indicating both p53-dependent and p53-independent mechanisms behind the synergy. APR-246 provides selectivity for TP53-mutated cells while NVB enhances p53-independent apoptosis and p53-dependent ferroptosis. Levels of ferroptosis induction correlate with the observed synergy in TP53-mutant and WT cells. Combination of APR-246 and NVB induces potent in vitro growth inhibition of primary TP53-mutated AML/CMML patient samples, with significant activity achieved at low micromolar or nanomolar concentrations of APR-246. Our findings hold promise for combination of APR-246 and NVB as a new therapeutic strategy tailored for TP53-mutated AML patients with high efficacy and low toxicity.

papers.title: Homoplastic evolution of proximal podomere patterning across Arthropoda
papers.abstract: The jointed arthropod leg is often credited as a key innovation spurring the evolutionary success of the phylum. Across lineages, each territory of the appendage has served as the substrate for myriad adaptations and structural innovations. While much of the available data has supported a conserved suite of transcription factors responsible for the initiation and patterning of the arthropod appendage, recent works have begun to highlight instances of lineage-specific shifts in expression dynamics, particularly amongst the chelicerates, correlated both with the emergence of novel structures and developmental system drift in the specification of plesiomorphic structures. These works confound efforts to align or homologize the leg segments across arthropod lineages, an effort already challenged by ground plan differences in segment number between the subphyla. An even more unusual architecture of leg segments occurs in sea spiders (Pycnogonida), which alone among Arthropoda are considered by systematists to bear three coxae (proximal segments), in contrast to the single coxa of the remaining arthropods. Here, we examined proximal podomere patterning in the developing appendages of a sea spider and an arachnid. We find that a particular spatial arrangement of Lim1 and SoxNeuro characterizes the developing coxa and trochanter of the harvestman Phalangium opilio (Opiliones) throughout appendage formation, with RNAi depletions of Lim1 yielding deletions of coxa and trochanter. Comparison of expression patterns across taxa shows that Lim1 and SoxNeuro have a similar spatial arrangement in the harvestman and sea spider, but these suggest conflicting interpretations of leg segment homology. We show that this is attributable to homoplastic patterns of evolution in SoxNeuro across Arthropoda. Expanding our surveys of prominent PD axis-patterning transcription factors supports additional instances of homoplasy in the domains of Sp6-9 and Irx2. The pervasiveness of homoplasy in gene expression patterns demands measured skepticism of homology statements and careful comparisons of multiple patterning genes, toward achieving falsifiability in the homology of structures.

papers.title: Fertilization offsets the maternal age effect on mouse oocytes provided the oviduct is not itself aged
papers.abstract: Advanced maternal age compromises oocyte quality, and it is widely assumed that these deficits are transmitted to embryos. However, because most studies rely on in vivo conception, it has been difficult to separate the effects of oocyte aging from those of an aged fertilization environment. In aging mice, we observed that the fraction of ovulated oocytes forming implantation sites after in vivo conception fell ~3.7-fold, raising the question of whether this was due to reduced fertilization, reduced embryo quality or reduced support from the aged reproductive tract. Therefore we fertilized oocytes of aged and young mice in vitro with a shared young-donor sperm preparation, holding the fertilization environment constant and removing paternal variability. Hallmarks of maternal age were largely offset following fertilization in vitro: aged oocytes produced blastocysts at rates comparable to young controls, with altered - but not deficient - cell-lineage composition and no detectable impairment in development to term (E18.5) after transfer to young oviducts. Proteomic analysis revealed that, unlike the transcriptomic signature, the proteomic age signature of oocytes was not faithfully propagated to the blastocyst: for a subset of proteins, particularly those depleted in aged oocytes, the direction of the age effect reversed between oocyte and blastocyst. Comparison with parthenogenetically activated oocytes showed this divergence to be fertilization-dependent, implicating fertilization - rather than mere embryonic cleavage - as the driver of proteomic change. Stable-isotope labelling in live embryos showed that blastocysts from aged, fertilized oocytes both synthesized more new protein and retained less maternal protein than young counterparts; neither effect was detectable after parthenogenesis. Puromycin labelling, by contrast, showed a maternal-age-associated rise in bulk synthesis regardless of route. Together, these results indicate that the maternal-age effect on the oocyte proteome is labile rather than fixed and can be offset by fertilization itself, provided the maternal environment is not itself aged.

papers.title: HNRNPC-mediated RNA processing promotes VHL-associated excessive vasculogenesis in von Hippel-Lindau syndrome revealed from patient-derived blood vessel models
papers.abstract: Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome (VHLS) is an inherited disorder characterized by excessive vascularization, which contributes to the development of hemangioblastomas and benign or malignant tumors, as well as renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and cysts in multiple organs. VHLS is caused by mutations in VHL tumor suppressor gene, which encodes a component of an E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. Although therapeutic agents targeting hypoxia-inducible factor 2 alpha (HIF2A), which is stabilized by VHL loss and promotes tumor angiogenesis, have been approved for clinical use, their therapeutic response remains limited in RCC patients associated with VHLS. Therefore, there is an unmet need for the development of alternative therapeutic approaches independent of HIF2A. Here, we establish a human iPSCs-based model of VHLS-associated excessive vasculogenesis using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from VHLS patients and VHL-edited isogenic iPSC lines. Vascular cells (VCs) differentiated from these VHLS-specific iPSCs exhibited excessive blood vessel formation compared to healthy donor-derived VCs, leading to vascular lesion formation characterized by abundant blood vessels and abnormal cellular growth in vivo. Mechanistically, RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) were preferentially stabilized in the patient-VCs. Among these RBPs, the stabilization of heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C1/C2 (HNRNPC), which is a substrate for pVHL-mediated protein degradation independent of HIF2A expression, was critical for the dysregulated vascularization caused by VHL inactivation in this model. These findings provide an iPSCs-derived vascular platform to elucidate VHLS mechanisms and identify HNRNPC as a potential therapeutic target for VHL-driven vascular lesion formations through an HIF2A-independent mechanism.

papers.title: Tiled base editing screens uncover rare second-site mutations that rescue a misfolded disease protein
papers.abstract: Therapeutic base editing can directly revert ~30% of disease-causing missense mutations to the wild-type sequence. One strategy to broaden its reach is to install second-site corrector mutations that improve protein stability or function across multiple pathogenic alleles. Here, we use tiled adenine and cytosine base editing screens to identify such corrector mutations in NPC1, a lysosomal cholesterol transporter whose misfolding causes Niemann-Pick type C disease. Tiling mutagenesis of the endogenous NPC1 locus in haploid human cells carrying the prevalent NPC1I1061T disease allele, combined with phenotypic reporters for cholesterol transport and protein abundance, uncovered rare intragenic suppressor mutations distributed across multiple domains. Unexpectedly, we identified a promiscuous second-site variant that can correct many different pathogenic NPC1 mutations. These correctors improve protein stability, promote ER exit and lysosomal trafficking, and restore cholesterol clearance in patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons. Our results establish in situ base editing screens for the discovery of second-site corrector mutations that are actionable for therapeutic base editing when the original mutation cannot be corrected.

papers.title: Conformation governs cellular behaviors of LRRK2 Parkinson's disease variants
papers.abstract: Gain-of-function of leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is a common cause of Parkinson's disease (PD). In its autoinhibited state, the leucine-rich repeats of LRRK2 block the kinase active site, preventing substrate phosphorylation. Displacing the repeats ('unlatching') primes LRRK2 for activity. Preferential unlatching causes increased substrate phosphorylation of the PD allele LRRK2[R1441H], but not LRRK2[G2019S]. Here, we define a large class of PD-associated 'unlatching' mutations based on their effect on LRRK2 conformation. Unlatching mutants show increased localization to membranes, the site of LRRK2's Rab substrates. Unlatching mutants are also characterized by decreased LRRK2 S935 phosphorylation, which we define as a biomarker of conformation. This framework resolves the mechanism of variants such as I2020T, which structural studies could not predict. Overall, we establish unlatching as a unifying mechanism for most PD-linked variants and describe measurable readouts for identifying LRRK2-driven disease.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal mapping of endothelial proliferative response in acute chemical liver injury
papers.abstract: Endothelial cells are major contributors to liver injury response, regeneration, and chronic liver disease. Previous studies identified a proliferative endothelial response to acute liver injury; however, a comprehensive characterization of this adaptive response is missing. We have developed a novel pipeline for spatiotemporal analysis of proliferative response in the liver. We demonstrate that endothelial cells enter the cell cycle upon acute centrilobular injury with a delay compared to hepatocytes and in a spatially distinct pattern from hepatocytes. We show that endothelial cycling predominantly occurs in the pericentral zone, while hepatocyte cycling occurs uniformly throughout the lobule. Endothelial cycling in injured livers leads to heightened clonal expansion, and to serial division rarely observed in homeostatic livers. Consequently, injured lobules exhibit endothelial overabundance during regeneration. Our study provides an in-depth characterization of endothelial proliferative response to liver injury and establishes a novel pipeline for spatiotemporal mapping of hepatic cell states.

papers.title: Mechanotransduction tuned by intermediate filaments promotes DNA repair in stiff environments
papers.abstract: High mammographic density increases breast cancer risk. Dense tissues are rich in fibrillar collagen, forming a rigid extracellular matrix around the epithelium. Although cancer initiation and progression are closely tied to DNA damage and to the DNA damage response, if and how tissue stiffness affects genome maintenance is not fully elucidated. We found that repair factor recruitment is more efficient, and that DNA breaks are repaired faster by cells on rigid substrates. Mechanistically, hemidesmosomal integrins, intermediate filaments, the LINC complex, and YAP are key mediators of this mechanogenomic response. Rigid tissue contexts favor survival of cells with DNA damage, which may lead to the accumulation of somatic mutations, as identified here with RNAseq analyses of normal breast tissue. Our findings provide new insights into how tissue rigidity influences cancer risk.

papers.title: Single-probe, amplification-free multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH maps bacterial gene expression in intact three-dimensional biofilms
papers.abstract: Biofilms are spatially structured communities in which local microenvironments drive physiological differentiation, yet mapping gene expression inside intact three-dimensional biofilms remains challenging. Bacterial spatial transcriptomics methods typically rely on tiled probe sets, sequential hybridization rounds, or signal amplification. Here, we show that a single short, directly labelled peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe per target is sufficient to quantify bacterial mRNA in situ without amplification. With all probes designed for a common hybridization condition, a transcript panel is resolved in one hybridization on a standard confocal microscope, in unmodified cells while preserving biofilm architecture. Benchmarked against the biphasic cycle of Legionella pneumophila, multiplex mRNA PNA-FISH recovers the expected transcriptional switch and agrees quantitatively with RT-qPCR in planktonic and biofilm populations. In flow-cell biofilms, it shows that sessile populations do not recapitulate the planktonic program and that transcriptional differences follow cellular aggregation state rather than depth.

papers.title: XRN1-dependent RNA homeostasis regulates hepatitis D virus
papers.abstract: Hepatitis delta virus (HDV) infection causes the most severe form of viral hepatitis, yet the host mechanisms restricting HDV replication remain poorly understood. Although HDV infection activates the MDA5-LGP2 pathway and induces robust interferon (IFN) responses, these antiviral programs have limited impact on viral replication. Here we identify the 5-3 exoribonuclease XRN1 as a key regulator of HDV infection. Loss of XRN1 in hepatoma cells increased double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) levels and induced interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs), including MDA5 and MAVS, and limited HDV infection. XRN1 deficiency enhanced ADAR1-mediated RNA editing, revealing a dynamic interplay between endogenous dsRNA metabolism and antiviral sensing. Inhibition of type I IFN signaling restored MDA5 expression and rescued HDV replication in XRN1-deficient cells. To identify the downstream effectors responsible for this restriction, we combined transcriptomic profiling with functional siRNA screening and identified DUSP5 and SIRPA as previously unrecognized ISGs with anti-HDV activity. Together, our findings establish XRN1 as a gatekeeper of dsRNA homeostasis that controls HDV replication through innate immune activation and reveals host antiviral effectors that may provide therapeutic opportunities for chronic hepatitis D.

papers.title: Generation of functional adipoids from human induced pluripotent stem cells
papers.abstract: Human adipose tissue models are lacking although essential for metabolic research. Traditional primary cell cultures are poorly scalable and unsuitable for drug screening or modeling of genetic disease. Conventional two-dimensional adipocyte cultures cannot withstand the long-term treatment required to mimic chronic conditions such as obesity and insulin resistance. To overcome these limitations, we developed an accessible protocol to produce three-dimensional human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived adipocyte microtissues, termed adipoids. hiPSC-derived adipoids display long-term stability and viability. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing revealed that adipoids contain mature adipocytes and adipocyte stem/progenitor cells, similar to human adipose tissue. Furthermore, hiPSC-derived adipoids contain unilocular adipocytes, exhibit stimulated lipolysis, and secrete adipokines. Thus, hiPSC-derived adipoids provide a functional, scalable and genetically tractable model to perform large-scale pharmacological screens and to investigate human metabolic disease.

papers.title: Genomic context tunes sequence-encoded RNA processing
papers.abstract: Sequence and genomic position jointly determine RNA processing, but at native loci the two are difficult to separate. Here, we uncoupled them by integrating RNA-processing elements into endogenous transcription units at tens of thousands of mapped positions and different elements at shared positions. Genomic position dominated RNA production levels but differentially influenced RNA processing events. A cryptic polyadenylation site, used natively only upon U1 inhibition, was rarely used ectopically. In contrast, introns partially retained at their native loci remained so across thousands of ectopic positions, with a substantial fraction of transcripts reaching the cytoplasm unspliced. SON depletion reduced splicing of two such introns, preferentially near speckles. Chromatin state, GC content, and speckle proximity tuned this behavior without overriding it, and in opposite directions: speckle proximity improved the splicing of one intron and reduced that of another. Specialized introns are therefore portable modules carrying their own processing information.

papers.title: The Global Phosphorylation Landscape of Acute Heat Stress in Reef-Building Corals
papers.abstract: Warming oceans disrupt the coral-algal symbiosis that sustains reefs, yet the signaling mechanisms initiating bleaching remain poorly understood. Integrating global phosphoproteomics across three reef-building corals with protein structure modeling revealed conservation between coral and human kinases, enabling inference of coral kinase activities and uncovering a shared signaling program induced by acute heat stress. Heat rapidly activated ERK, JNK, and p38 MAP kinases, suppressed cell cycle signaling, and remodeled pathways controlling chromatin, RNA processing, and metabolism. Most strikingly, thermal stress rewired immune receptor signaling networks associated with non-self recognition, suggesting that heat shifts the coral host from tolerance to immune recognition of its algal symbionts. These findings define conserved signaling mechanisms that precede bleaching, revealing actionable molecular targets for enhancing coral resilience.

papers.title: Uncovering disease progression trajectories across multiple timescales with hybrid ODE-mixture models
papers.abstract: Biological systems are capable of evolving across multiple timescales, yet most modeling approaches capture either short-term physiological responses or long-term disease progression. Additionally, methods that combine these time scales either struggle with inter-individual variation, or require large volumes of data to work. We present Latent Class Parameter Trajectory Analysis (LCPTA), a hybrid framework that combines mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE) modeling of short-term dynamics with latent class trajectory modeling of long-term parameter evolution. To support this approach, we developed TemporalMixtureModels.jl, a Julia package for univariate and multivariate temporal mixture modeling. We evaluated LCPTA in two synthetic longitudinal studies, covering a simulation of a heterogeneous population developing hypertension, as well as a synthetic longitudinal study of 75 virtual individuals followed over 30 years, representing muscle insulin resistance, liver insulin resistance, and healthy trajectories. We compared LCPTA with a conditional neural ODE and a conditional neural network for reconstruction of long-term parameter trajectories and subgroup separation. In both studies LCPTA recovered relevant subgroup structure and trajectory patterns. In the cardiovascular study, the neural approaches were able to distinguish inter-individual differences, but in the insulin sensitivity study, neural approaches failed to represent parameter trajectories faithfully, primarily separating individuals along a single dominant parameter and showing weaker multivariate trajectory reconstruction. In additional experiments with sparse and irregularly sampled unseen individuals, LCPTA maintained strong classification performance. We show that LCPTA is an efficient and interpretable strategy for multiscale modeling of heterogeneous metabolic disease progression, with potential utility for data-efficient digital twin applications.

papers.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships1. Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

papers.title: Photosynthesis-derived carbohydrate supply sustains CuCl2-induced phytoalexin production in rice leaves
papers.abstract: Phytoalexins are antimicrobial metabolites whose biosynthesis is triggered by signaling activated by both biotic and abiotic elicitors, but the physiological conditions that sustain their production remain poorly understood. Here, we examined how light and carbohydrate availability affect CuCl2-induced production of diterpenoid (phytocassanes and momilactones) and flavonoid (sakuranetin) phytoalexins in rice (Oryza sativa L.) leaf disks. Darkness strongly suppressed both the accumulation of all three phytoalexin groups and the induction of their biosynthetic genes. In darkness, endogenous sucrose, glucose, and fructose declined to 3%-8% of the levels in the light, whereas early accumulation of jasmonic acid and jasmonoyl-L-isoleucine (JA-Ile) was not detectably reduced. Exogenous sucrose restored phytoalexin accumulation in darkness in a dose-dependent manner, together with the expression of the suppressed biosynthetic genes, whereas equimolar mannitol had no effect. Glucose also restored sakuranetin accumulation in darkness but only partially restored diterpenoid accumulation, whereas the glucose analog 2-deoxy-D-glucose did not, and it suppressed CuCl2-induced accumulation in the light in a dose-dependent manner. In the light, 3-(3,4-dichlorophenyl)-1,1-dimethylurea (DCMU), an inhibitor of photosynthetic electron transport, depleted soluble sugars and suppressed phytoalexin accumulation, and sucrose reversed this suppression. Sugars alone induced little phytoalexin accumulation, indicating that carbohydrates act permissively rather than as elicitors. Diterpenoid phytoalexins depended more strongly on light than sakuranetin, yet both classes depended on carbohydrate availability. These results indicate that photosynthesis-derived carbohydrate supply sustains elicitor-induced phytoalexin production in rice leaves and largely accounts for its light dependence.

papers.title: TROP2 and immune gene expression by African ancestry in triple-negative breast cancer
papers.abstract: Purpose: TROP2 is a treatment target in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). TACSTD2 encodes TROP2, while PDCD1 encodes the immune protein PD-1. We investigated whether these genes differ by race or African genetic ancestry and whether the reported link between higher TACSTD2 and lower immune-gene expression partly reflects the mixture of cells in tumor samples. Methods: We analyzed TNBC tumors from TCGA (n = 107) and GSE268851 (n = 253; ancestry data for 229), together with spatial, normal-breast, and protein datasets. Regression models adjusted for age, tumor stage, and a score based on epithelial gene expression. We compared TACSTD2 with other epithelial markers using paired bootstrap analysis. Results: TACSTD2 was detected in nearly all tumors, with no significant differences by race or ancestry. Higher African ancestry was linked to higher PDCD1 expression in TCGA (P = 0.00039), but not in GSE268851. In GSE268851, higher TACSTD2 remained associated with lower CD8A, GZMB, and cytotoxic score after epithelial adjustment (all q < 0.003). These associations were stronger than those for EPCAM; the CD8A association was also stronger than that for KRT8. TACSTD2 was 1.55-fold higher in TNBC than in normal breast and correlated with TROP2 protein (Spearman rho = 0.74). Conclusion: TACSTD2 was widely expressed in the TNBC groups studied, while the ancestry-PDCD1 association differed between cohorts. Epithelial gene expression did not fully explain some negative TACSTD2-immune associations, and some were stronger than those for other epithelial markers such as EPCAM.

papers.title: Age-based shifts in multicellular community organization and abundance in HPV-Negative Head and Neck Cancer
papers.abstract: Aging represents a fundamental driver of cancer risk and progression, yet the mechanisms by which aging reshapes the tumor microenvironment remain incompletely understood. To interrogate how aging alters cellular and microenvironmental organization in cancer, we developed an integrated single-cell atlas of HPV-negative head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) encompassing 73 patients aged 18-91 years. Using a multi-layered computational framework combining NMF-based module discovery and partial correlation network analysis, we reveal that age-associated differences in tumor composition are driven primarily by selective shifts in cell type abundance and organization rather than widespread age-dependent transcriptional rewiring. We identify an age-enriched cellular community centered on basal-like squamous epithelial states linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, matrix-associated myofibroblast-like CAFs, and FOLR2+ macrophages, which secrete immunosuppressive and ECM-remodeling factors. Cross-dataset in-silico validation via TCGA transcriptomes, spatial transcriptomics, and mouse tumor models confirms the correlation of these cell types across patients, specific ligand-receptor usage, and increased proportions of epithelial and stromal cells in aged mouse models. Among epithelial cell-intrinsic age-associated transcriptional changes, midkine (MDK) emerges as a rare but robust tumor-derived signal linked to stromal remodeling, immunosuppression, and invasive epithelial programs. These findings reveal conserved mechanisms of age-dependent cellular reorganization in the tumor microenvironment and identify MDK and associated stromal-remodeling pathways as potential intervention points for age-stratified cancer therapy.

papers.title: Repeated Transitions in Migratory Behavior Across a Songbird Radiation Are Not Driven by Selection on Shared Variation in Candidate Genes
papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms facilitating the repeated evolution of traits is a core question in evolutionary biology. While repeated evolution has been observed across many systems, behavioral phenotypes have been less well studied than morphological traits. Migration is a behavioral adaptation to seasonality that has evolved independently in many animals, and repeated gains and losses of migratory behavior have been especially prevalent throughout the diversification of birds. While migratory traits are heritable in many taxa and candidate genes underlying intraspecific variation in migratory behavior have been identified, whether similar genetic changes are responsible for the repeated evolution of migration remains poorly understood. We used a phylogenomic approach to investigate the relationship between variation in candidate genes and migratory propensity across nearly all species in the parulid warbler radiation (n = 101), a group of songbirds in which migratory behavior has been lost and gained multiple times. Comparisons of candidate gene tree topologies to the parulid warbler species tree revealed cases of discordance, though these were explained by differences in the number of phylogenetically informative sites among genes rather than by elevated genetic similarity among species sharing migratory strategies. Testing models of coding sequence evolution identified sites with elevated dN/dS in five candidate genes, suggestive of positive selection; however, variation at these sites showed no clear association with migratory strategy, nor did we detect recurrent selection across lineages where transitions in migratory behavior most likely occurred. Together, these results contradict the hypothesis that selection on shared variation (ancestral polymorphisms or introgressed alleles) facilitated the repeated evolution of migration in this clade.

papers.title: BSG.S regulates ionocyte radial intercalation and function in the developing Xenopus mucociliary epithelium.
papers.abstract: Mucociliary epithelia (MCE) line multiple vertebrate organs, including the mammalian airways, and rely on coordinated interactions among specialized cell types to clear pathogens and maintain epithelial homeostasis. Proper MCE function requires the appropriate specification and spatial organization of ionocytes, multiciliated cells, secretory cells, and basal cells. Ionocytes regulate ion transport and pH homeostasis, yet the mechanisms governing their integration and function within the developing epithelium remain incompletely understood. Basigin (BSG), also known as CD147 or EMMPRIN, is a conserved transmembrane glycoprotein implicated in cell migration, adhesion, and signaling. However, its role in mucociliary epithelial development remains unclear. Here, we show that the short isoform of BSG (BSG.S) is expressed in ionocytes of the Xenopus laevis MCE. Our findings demonstrate that BSG.S depletion impairs ionocyte radial intercalation, alters intracellular pH, and disrupts epithelial organization. Furthermore, BSG.S loss alters epithelial cell-type composition, decreasing the number of basal cells and increasing the number of multiciliated cells. These findings suggest BSG.S as a regulator of ionocyte integration, epithelial organization, and cell-type composition during mucociliary epithelial development.

papers.title: Molecular dissection of the ChAHP complex subunits Adnp and Chd4 reveals common and divergent functions in retinal development
papers.abstract: Epigenetic remodelling is thought to regulate the progression of competence states in neural progenitor cells. Here, we examined the functions of the ChAHP chromatin remodelling complex during retinal development. ChAHP consists of the ATP-dependent nucleosome remodeller CHD4, the zinc finger and homeodomain transcription factor ADNP, and the HP1 heterochromatin proteins (Cbx1/3/5). Notably, both CHD4 and ADNP are genetically associated with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), but ChAHP functions in neural development are not fully understood. In the retina, we found that both ADNP and CHD4 proteins were co-expressed ubiquitously in each cell type throughout development, and the two proteins formed a complex in vivo. Next, we generated retina-specific conditional knockouts (cKOs) to both Adnp and Chd4 using the Chx10-Cre driver. We observed phenotypic correspondence and divergence. Developmentally, we observed elevated cell death in both Adnp and Chd4 cKOs, but Adnp cKOs also exhibited deficits in progenitor numbers and proliferation. As a result, mature Adnp cKOs were hypoplastic with reductions in each cell type. We previously described a more complex phenotype in Chd4 cKOs, where cell fates were imbalanced and progenitor proliferation was prolonged, but these features were absent from the Adnp cKO. To understand how ChAHP regulates gene expression, we compared Adnp and Chd4 cKOs via scRNA-seq, which revealed common transcriptional signatures. However, Chd4 cKOs exhibited more severe effects on gene expression in line with its stronger effects on cell fate. We then performed cut&run-seq, which suggested that Adnp and Chd4 are recruited to the same genomic loci - many of which are also occupied by the Ctcf transcription factor. Taken together, our data suggest that ChAHP regulates retinal growth, but that CHD4 has additional ChAHP-independent functions in regulating progenitor fate decisions. These findings point to the idea that during neurogenesis, some brain regions may have greater dependence on ChAHP, and therefore greater vulnerability to genetic mutation.

papers.title: Modeling ATN1 mutations in human iPSCs reveals early developmental roles of atrophin-1
papers.abstract: Atrophin-1 (ATN1), encoded by the ATN1 gene, is an evolutionarily conserved transcriptional corepressor implicated in neuronal development and severe incurable disorders, including the polyglutamine (polyQ) disease - dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA), and the neurodevelopmental syndrome CHEDDA. However, the cellular function of ATN1 and its role during early human development remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we generated an isogenic panel of human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines, establishing a novel resource for comprehensive studies of ATN1 function and dysfunction. This panel includes a DRPLA patient-derived line (wt/mut), CRISPR-Cas9-corrected wild-type controls (wt/wt), complete ATN1 knock-out clones (-/-), and heterozygous lines expressing either a wild-type or a mutant allele (wt/- and -/mut). While pluripotency markers remained unaffected across all variants, further characterization revealed marked proliferation deficits in ATN1 knock-out lines and heterozygous iPSCs without wild-type allele expression. Moreover, the formation of punctate ATN1 assemblies was enhanced in iPSCs with -/mut variants. The pronounced phenotype observed in cells expressing only the mutant ATN1 allele may result from a combination of loss-of-function and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms. Overall, the generated panel of iPSC lines provides a unique cellular platform for investigating ATN1-dependent molecular mechanisms and their contribution to neuronal development and disease.

papers.title: Cannabidiol Impairs Glucagon Trafficking and Secretion Through the Lysosomal System in Murine αTC1-6 cells
papers.abstract: Glucagon secretion by pancreatic cells is regulated by nutrient, paracrine, and neural inputs, and emerging evidence suggests that the islet endocannabinoid system (ECS) may also regulate -cell function. While phytocannabinoids such as cannabidiol (CBD) have been shown to interact with the ECS, and negatively regulate insulin secretion from pancreatic {beta} cells, whether CBD alters cell function in ways that disrupt glucagon trafficking and secretion remains unclear. This study investigates how acute CBD exposure affects transcriptional and secretory networks governing cell function. Using the TC1-6 glucagon-secreting cell line, we exposed the cells to 0.3 and 3 M CBD for RT-qPCR analysis, 3 M CBD for bulk RNA sequencing, and 3 M CBD or its inactive metabolite 7-COOH-CBD for imaging and secretion experiments. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that treatment with CBD did not alter the expression of ECS receptors and enzymes. However, pathways involved in cellular excitability, peptide hormone trafficking, and secretion were significantly downregulated. Using confocal microscopy, we found that CBD exposure increased the colocalization of glucagon with LAMP1 (a lysosomal marker), and that CBD rerouted peripheral glucagon, and glucagon-containing lysosomes towards the intracellular region of the cell. In conjunction with these findings, we observed reduced glucose-stimulated glucagon secretion under high glucose conditions. Overall, our data supports a model in which acute CBD exposure downregulates processes governing cellular excitability and peptide secretion and negatively regulates glucagon trafficking and secretion by rerouting peripheral glucagon into lysosome-associated intracellular compartments in TC1-6 cells.

papers.title: Gαq-mediated contact release is required for efficient mitochondrial quality control
papers.abstract: Lysosomes and mitochondria are highly dynamic organelles whose coordinated interactions are essential for cellular homeostasis, while their dysfunction contributes to numerous human diseases. Here, we identify the mitochondrial outer membrane protein Fis1 and the RabGAPs TBC1D15 and TBC1D17 as novel interacting partners of the heterotrimeric G protein -subunit Gq. Using mitochondrial proteomics, co-immunoprecipitation, proximity ligation assays, and in vitro binding studies with purified proteins, we demonstrate that Gq forms a complex with Fis1 and TBC1D15/TBC1D17 through a non-canonical interaction interface. Gq localizes to mitochondria-lysosome contact sites, where it regulates the dynamic balance between contact formation and dissociation. Loss of Gq resulted in enlarged and clustered lysosomes and increased the extent and duration of mitochondria-lysosome contacts. Live-cell imaging revealed prolonged organelle tethering in Gq-deficient cells, while proximity ligation and three-dimensional reconstruction analyses localized Gq and TBC1D15 to mitochondrial tips closely associated with lysosomes. This localization, together with increased mitochondrial fission and altered mitophagic turnover following Gq loss, links the regulation of contacts at mitochondrial tips to mitochondrial fragmentation and quality control. Re-expression of Gq, but not the non-canonical interaction-deficient mutant, restored normal lysosomal morphology, contact-site dynamics, mitochondrial fragmentation, and mitophagy. Together, these findings identify a Gq as a dynamic regulator of mitochondria-lysosome untethering and connect contact site turnover with mitochondria fragmentation and mitophagy. Our work uncovers a novel link between G protein signaling, organelle communication, and mitochondrial quality control.

papers.title: Mitotic centromeres organize in repeat-subunits with specialized histone landscape and multi-domain architecture as revealed by expansion microscopy
papers.abstract: Centromeres ensure faithful chromosome segregation during cell division, yet their underlying architecture and spatial arrangement of centromeric proteins remain incompletely resolved. Here, we apply Ten-fold Robust Expansion Microscopy (TREx) to human diploid hTERT RPE-1 cells to visualize mitotic centromeres at nanoscale resolution. We find that the centromeric histone variant CENP-A and the kinetochore protein KNL1 form discontinuous, repeating substructures. We further resolve centromeric chromatin into four spatially distinct domains: an inner kinetochore domain marked by CENP-A, a mantle domain marked by RAD21, an outer core domain marked by CENP-B, and a distinct, RAD21-associated inner centromere domain. Core and pericentromeric regions share a specialized chromatin landscape, extending the concept of centrochromatin, with enrichment of H3S10ph and H3K9me3, depletion of H3K27me3, and low-level enrichment of the euchromatic marks H3K4me3 and H3K36me3. Together, we uncover a discontinuous repeat-subunit organization and multidomain architecture of the human centromere that combines euchromatic and heterochromatic modifications.

papers.title: Pathological levels of α-synuclein increase basal mitophagy in Parkinson's dopamine neurons
papers.abstract: Elevated -synuclein results in mitochondrial dysfunction, however the exact mechanism is poorly understood. -Synuclein localises to multiple subcellular sites including mitochondria, where it binds anionic lipids which regulate mitochondrial dynamics through DRP1. We hypothesised that pathogenic levels of -synuclein lead to dysregulation of mitophagy and lipid-dependent mitochondrial dynamics, causing mitochondrial and neuronal dysfunction. Using induced pluripotent stem cell-dopamine neurons (iPSC-DANs) carrying the -synuclein gene triplication mutation (SNCA-Trp) which causes an early-onset form of Parkinson's disease (PD), we established that elevated -synuclein increased basal mitophagy compared to healthy controls and overall loss of mitochondrial mass. This was associated with accumulation of basal mitophagy receptors BNIP3 and NIX and decreased proteasome activity, and was independent of PINK1-Parkin mitophagy. We identified reduced mitochondrial gene expression by single cell RNAseq, mirroring heightened mitophagy and mitochondrial depletion. We found increased levels of DRP1-dependent mitochondrial fission and perturbed levels of anionic lipids, including cardiolipin and phosphatidic acid, two lipids which directly bind to -synuclein. Pharmacological inhibition of DRP1 reversed the excessive basal mitophagy in SNCA-Trp neurons and restored deficits in cellular ATP and calcium release. Finally, we assessed neuronal function and found that impairment of mitochondrial dysfunction by elevated -synuclein led to reductions in neuronal firing activity. Inhibition of DRP1 rescued the neuronal activity deficit in SNCA-Trp neurons, suggesting that relieving - instead of increasing - mitophagy pressure may be beneficial in -synuclein-driven PD.

papers.title: The galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain maintains plasma membrane phosphatidylserine required for KRAS function
papers.abstract: KRAS is a small GTPase essential for cellular proliferation, differentiation, and survival. It is predominantly localized to the plasma membrane (PM), where it forms nanoclusters essential for signal transduction. This PM binding and nanoclustering strictly depend on phosphatidylserine (PtdSer), an anionic phospholipid enriched in the inner PM leaflet. Galectin-3 (Gal-3), a {beta}-galactoside-binding lectin implicated in cell growth, migration and tumor progression, has been shown to regulate KRAS PM binding and nanoclustering. Here, we demonstrate that Gal-3 knockout (KO) or inhibition of its carbohydrate recognition domain (CRD) depletes KRAS and PtdSer from the PM. Exogenous PtdSer supplementation fully restores PM PtdSer and partially restores KRAS PM binding, indicating that Gal-3 promotes KRAS PM binding in part by maintaining PM PtdSer content. Total cellular PtdSer, PM PI4P, cholesterol and GM3 are unchanged, excluding these established regulators of PM PtdSer. Instead, Gal-3 CRD inhibition disrupts the cellular balance of sphingomyelin (SM) and ceramide, alters intracellular SM distribution, and impairs the endocytic and recycling transport of PtdSer, SM, and epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR). Together, our findings demonstrate that Gal-3 CRD activity sustains PM PtdSer content through endocytic trafficking, providing the PM lipid composition required for KRAS PM spatial organization.
